keyTakeaways: All Hallows' Eve is 31 October, the vigil that opens All Saints' Day on 1 November; in 2026 it is a Saturday, in 2027 a Sunday.

faqs.question: Is All Hallows' Eve the same as Halloween?
faqs.answer: Yes, they name the same night, 31 October. Halloween is the shortened form of All Hallows' Eve; the longer phrase keeps its church sense as the vigil that opens All Saints' Day on 1 November.

faqs.question: Why is it called All Hallows' Eve?
faqs.answer: Because it is the eve of All Hallows, the feast of all the saints together. In Old English the feast was ealra hálgena mæssedæg, all saints' mass-day, and hálga was the ordinary noun for a saint.

faqs.question: Why don't English speakers call saints hallows any more?
faqs.answer: French-derived saint replaced it. A 2018 study by Olga Timofeeva found saint used 1,164 times as a title in an early Middle English corpus; the noun halwe became obsolete after 1500 and survives only in names like All Hallows.

faqs.question: Where does the apostrophe go in All Hallows' Eve?
faqs.answer: After the s: All Hallows' Eve, because hallows is plural. In English books from 2015 to 2019 that spelling has 52.6% of uses; All Hallow's Eve, at 16.8%, wrongly means the eve of a single saint.

faqs.question: Why does a church feast begin the evening before?
faqs.answer: Medieval Christians counted a holy day from sunset to sunset. The Church of England keeps the rule: except for Christmas and Easter, a Principal Feast begins with Evening Prayer on the day before, using the feast's own collect.

faqs.question: What happens at an All Hallows' Eve church service?
faqs.answer: In the Episcopal Church's Book of Occasional Services (2003), the evening service begins by lighting lamps, then sets readings such as the Witch of Endor and Ezekiel's valley of dry bones, and ends with the Te Deum. Festivities may come before or after.

faqs.question: What dates are the three days of Allhallowtide in 2026 and 2027?
faqs.answer: In 2026: Saturday 31 October, Sunday 1 November and Monday 2 November. In 2027: Sunday 31 October, Monday 1 November and Tuesday 2 November. Church of England parishes may move All Saints to Sunday 31 October in 2027.

faqs.question: Is All Hallows' Eve meant to be a fast day?
faqs.answer: Traditionally it was a day of preparation. The Church of England's Common Worship rules still say the eves of Principal Feasts, All Saints' Day among them, are appropriately kept as days of discipline and self-denial.

faqs.question: What did Shakespeare call Halloween?
faqs.answer: All-hallond Eve. In Measure for Measure, Act 2, Scene 1, Master Froth corrects Pompey, who said his father died at Hallowmas. The -n form echoes an Old English genitive plural, of the saints.

faqs.question: Is All Hallows' Eve a religious or a secular occasion?
faqs.answer: The name and the date are liturgical, set by the feast of All Saints on 1 November. Costumes and trick-or-treating grew up around the night later, and some churches now hold a service on the eve itself.

article.contentMarkdown:
# All Hallows' Eve Meaning: The Phrase, the Vigil and the Three Days

All Hallows' Eve means the night that opens All Saints' Day: the eve of the hallows, or saints, taken all together. It is the old name for 31 October, the liturgical vigil before 1 November, and Halloween is its shortened form. "Hallows" comes from Old English *hálga*, a word that named a saint, and the eve counts because Christian feasts begin at evening prayer the night before.

The eve lands on a Saturday in 2026 and a Sunday in 2027, both 31 October. If you are explaining it to someone in a message, keep it short: phones account for 48.3% of the 57,456 views our SubhSandesh pages have recorded, and the median letter written on our "I miss you" pages runs to 88 words. Below: the grammar of the phrase, the words' paper trail, how the vigil works, the three days of Allhallowtide, and what churches still do on the night.

## What does All Hallows' Eve mean, word by word?

The phrase is a possessive: the eve belonging to All Hallows, which is the feast of every saint at once. Each of the three words carries a piece of that.

- **All**: every saint together, not one named saint. That is the point of the feast.
- **Hallows'**: the saints. In the [Bosworth-Toller Anglo-Saxon Dictionary entry for hálga](https://bosworthtoller.com/18037), the word is a masculine noun meaning "a saint", and the feast appears as *ealra hálgena mæssedæg*, "all saints' mass-day".
- **Eve**: the evening before, and in church terms the first part of the feast itself.

The apostrophe sits after the s because *hallows* is plural. Old English marked that with a genitive plural ending, *hálgena*, "of the saints", so the possessive was built into the word long before English used apostrophes.

## Why "hallow" stopped meaning saint: 950 uses, then French arrived

Linguist Olga Timofeeva traced what happened to Old English religious words after 1066, in a [2018 study in English Language and Linguistics](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/english-language-and-linguistics/article/survival-and-loss-of-old-english-religious-vocabulary-between-1150-and-1350/BA4EEFD39CCED022CB8A66093290FDC7). The noun *hālga* appears about 950 times in the Old English corpus she used, often enough to survive the Norman Conquest.

It survived, but lost its job. In an early Middle English corpus she found the French-derived *saint* 1,164 times as a title before a name, yet only 22 times as a noun on its own, where *halwe* still led with 88. The noun *halwe* became obsolete after 1500, and her table gives its last dictionary attestation as 1647.

So the title came first and the noun followed: people said "Saint Martin" for centuries while still calling the group "the hallows". Once *saint* won both roles, *hallow* as a noun was left only in fixed calendar names like All Hallows, which is why the phrase now sounds archaic and slightly mysterious.

## The phrase in old texts: 4 dated forms

The forms below show the phrase moving from Old English into Shakespeare's English. Each is dated and checked in a text we could open.

### c. 1000: *ealra hálgena mæssedæg* in Ælfric's Grammar

Bosworth-Toller quotes Ælfric's Grammar: "November se mónaþ onginþ on ealra hálgena mæssedæg", which it translates as "the month of November begins on All Saints' day". The feast already had a fixed date, 1 November, and a name built on *hálga*.

### 1083: the day after All Saints in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle

The same entry cites the Chronicle for 1083: "on ðone dæg æfter ealra hálgena mæssedæg", on the day after All Saints' mass-day. It is dated by the feast, which shows how ordinary the name was as a calendar marker.

### c. 1597: "All-hallown summer" in Henry IV, Part 1

Prince Hal mocks the ageing Falstaff with "farewell, All-hallown summer!", an Indian summer arriving late in the year. The *-n* is a fossil of that Old English genitive plural, still audible in the 1590s.

### c. 1604: "All-hallond Eve" in Measure for Measure

In [Measure for Measure, Act 2, Scene 1](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/1530), Pompey says Master Froth's father died "at Hallowmas", and Froth corrects him: "All-hallond Eve." The joke depends on the audience hearing the eve and the feast as different days, a distinction the play could take for granted.

## What is a vigil, and why does the feast start the night before?

A vigil is a watch kept before a feast; the word comes from Latin *vigilia*, wakefulness. Medieval Christians counted a holy day from sunset to sunset, so the evening of 31 October was the opening of All Saints' Day, not a separate occasion.

The Church of England still works this way. Its [Common Worship rules for the Christian year](https://www.churchofengland.org/prayer-and-worship/worship-texts-and-resources/common-worship/prayer-and-worship/worship-texts-and-resources/common-worship/churchs-year/rules) list All Saints' Day among 9 Principal Feasts and say that, except for Christmas and Easter, the feast "begins with Evening Prayer on the day before", using the feast's own collect.

The same rules say the eves of Principal Feasts are "appropriately kept as days of discipline and self denial". That is the older meaning of a vigil: a quiet, slightly austere evening of preparation, which makes the noisy secular night that grew from it an odd sort of descendant.

## Allhallowtide: how the three days fit together in 2026 and 2027

Allhallowtide is the name for the three days from the eve through All Souls. Each day has its own purpose, and the weekday changes how parishes keep them.

| Day | Date | 2026 | 2027 | What the day is for |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| All Hallows' Eve | 31 October | Saturday | Sunday | Vigil; the feast opens at Evening Prayer |
| All Saints' Day (All Hallows) | 1 November | Sunday | Monday | Principal Feast for all the saints |
| All Souls' Day | 2 November | Monday | Tuesday | Commemoration of the faithful departed |

The Common Worship rules let All Saints' Day move to the Sunday between 30 October and 5 November. In 2026 that is 1 November itself, so the eve and the feast line up neatly over one weekend.

In 2027 the nearest Sunday is 31 October, so a parish that moves the feast keeps All Saints on Halloween itself, with the vigil on Saturday 30 October. If you plan to attend, check your own church's notice for that year rather than assuming the eve is a separate service.

## How churches mark All Hallows' Eve today

Some churches give the eve its own service, not just a vigil for the next day. The Episcopal Church's [Book of Occasional Services, 2003 edition](https://archive.org/details/occasional-services-2003), includes a "Service for All Hallows' Eve" for the evening of 31 October, next to a separate vigil for All Saints.

Its rubric allows "suitable festivities and entertainments" before or after the service and suggests a visit to a cemetery. The service opens with lamps being lit, then sets readings that match the night's mood:

- the Witch of Endor, 1 Samuel 28:3-25, read in parts by a narrator and readers for Saul, the witch and Samuel;
- the vision of Eliphaz the Temanite, Job 4:12-21;
- the valley of dry bones, Ezekiel 37:1-14;
- the war in heaven, Revelation 12:7-12.

It closes with the Te Deum and the collect of All Saints' Day. That is the clearest sign we found that a church can hold the ghost story and the vigil in one evening; we read the 2003 text, not the current 2022 edition.

## All Hallows' Eve, All Hallows Eve or All Hallow's Eve?

Write **All Hallows' Eve**, with the apostrophe after the s. On 15 October 2026 we pulled yearly counts for the four spellings in English books published 2015 to 2019 from the [Ngram comparison of the four spellings](https://books.google.com/ngrams/graph?content=All+Hallows%27+Eve%2CAll+Hallows+Eve%2CAll+Hallow%27s+Eve%2CAll+Hallow+Eve&year_start=1800&year_end=2019&corpus=en-2019&smoothing=0).

- All Hallows' Eve: 52.6% of uses.
- All Hallows Eve, no apostrophe: 29.3%.
- All Hallow's Eve, the singular possessive: 16.8%, and wrong, because it means the eve of one saint.
- All Hallow Eve: 1.3%, down from 28.7% in 1900 to 1909.

The old name is not dying either. Uses of the four spellings combined were 4.0 times more frequent in 2015 to 2019 than in the 1950s, even though "Halloween" still outnumbers them by about 47 to 1.

## Sending something on the eve itself

If the old meaning matters to you, the eve is a natural evening to write to one person rather than send a party invite. For a light note, the [interactive Halloween card](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-halloween) holds six photos at most, lets you choose the word that glows on the jack-o'-lantern and hides your letter in a dark attic; it takes roughly 5 minutes to make.

For something closer to a ceremony, the [cinematic premium Halloween page](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-halloween-premium) holds 12 photos plus a recording of your voice of up to 60 seconds. Its optional unlock time keeps everything but their name and a countdown hidden until the hour you pick, so you could set it for dusk on 31 October, when the vigil traditionally starts; allow around 10 minutes.

If the person lives far away and the night is more about missing them than about ghosts, our [long-distance "I miss you" page](https://subhsandesh.in/missyou-gf) is the better match. Our pages average 11.1 views each, which suggests people go back to what they were sent.

### Where these pages fall short on the eve

Both Halloween pages are playful and finish on a "be my boo" question, which jars with grief on All Souls' Day. For a death in the family, a handwritten note, a lit candle or your parish's book of remembrance does the job better, and neither page stands in for a church service. Each is built for a single recipient, with English-only screens, and neither works as a group invitation.

- Timofeeva, O. (2018), English Language and Linguistics 22(2): 225-247, open access
- Shakespeare, Measure for Measure, Project Gutenberg
- Church of England, Common Worship: Rules to Order the Christian Year
